title: Sunburn
summary: Manage sunburn by identifying blistering or systemic illness that warrants urgent assessment, avoiding further ultraviolet exposure, and using layered photoprotection to prevent recurrent injury. Broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, and sun avoidance reduce ultraviolet-associated skin damage.
seoDescription: Physician-focused approach to sunburn assessment, escalation for severe injury, medication-related photosensitivity, and evidence-based ultraviolet protection.
clinicalQuestion: How should clinicians triage acute sunburn and prevent recurrent ultraviolet injury?
keyTakeaways: Treat extensive blistering, severe pain, or systemic symptoms as potentially severe cutaneous injury rather than uncomplicated erythema; assess promptly for complications and exclude alternative phototoxic or severe drug reactions.

Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher as one component of protection; only broad-spectrum products at this threshold protect against ultraviolet rays associated with skin-cancer risk and early skin aging. [1][2]
Prioritize physical avoidance and protective clothing alongside sunscreen, because ultraviolet exposure occurs year-round and on cloudy days. [1]

Review medications when the eruption is disproportionate, sharply photodistributed, or recurrent: topical retinoids and systemic isotretinoin labeling warns of photosensitivity and increased susceptibility to sunburn. [5][6]
Do not apply sunscreen to infants younger than 6 months without clinician guidance. [1]

sections.heading: Triage acute sunburn for severe injury and alternative diagnoses
sections.intro: Classify the presentation before treating it as routine uncomplicated sunburn.
paragraphs: Document exposure timing, anatomic distribution, blistering, skin pain, peeling, ocular symptoms, and systemic complaints. Acute phototoxic eruptions can begin hours to days after ultraviolet exposure and may range from sunburn-like erythema and peeling to severe blistering in exposed sites. [16] A sharply photodistributed or unexpectedly severe reaction should trigger a medication and topical-product review rather than attribution to exposure duration alone.

Escalate same-day assessment for extensive blistering, uncontrolled pain, systemic illness, or concern for a serious cutaneous adverse reaction. Sunburn severe enough for burn-service admission is uncommon, whereas most cases are self-managed with simple creams and analgesics; this contrast supports escalation when injury exceeds the usual limited erythematous presentation. [10]

In children, use a lower threshold for evaluation because burns may be more severe than in adults. [2] For infants younger than 6 months, do not recommend sunscreen without consultation with a health professional. [1]
bullets: Ask specifically about topical tretinoin, adapalene, or tazarotene; all are associated with ultraviolet/environmental exposure warnings and photosensitivity or sunburn risk. [5]

Ask about oral isotretinoin and concomitant tetracyclines. Isotretinoin labeling identifies increased sunburn susceptibility and advises avoiding concomitant tetracyclines because of intracranial-hypertension risk. [6]
If the patient uses topical diclofenac gel, stop it at the first evidence of sunburn per prescribing information. [3]

sections.heading: Identify treatments that amplify ultraviolet injury
sections.intro: A medication review is most useful when severity or recurrence is discordant with reported exposure.
paragraphs: Topical retinoid counseling should include sun-exposure precautions at initiation and during dose escalation. Tretinoin labeling identifies skin irritation and photosensitivity with sunburn risk; adapalene labeling warns about ultraviolet and environmental exposure; and tazarotene labeling identifies photosensitivity and sunburn risk. [5] In a patient with retinoid dermatitis plus sunburn-like erythema, distinguish additive irritant dermatitis from a predominantly photo-induced reaction because both require reducing ultraviolet exposure.

For isotretinoin, counsel that sunburn and photosensitizing/photoallergic reactions are reported adverse effects, including increased susceptibility to sunburn. [6] New severe skin symptoms during isotretinoin require assessment for serious skin reactions; the label directs monitoring for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and other serious skin reactions. [6]

Do not reflexively label every sun-exposed eruption as simple sunburn. Severe blistering after ultraviolet exposure can occur in cutaneous drug reactions, and a recurrent pattern despite protective behavior should prompt reassessment of prescribed, over-the-counter, and topical agents. [16]
bullets: For topical diclofenac gel, discontinue at the first evidence of sunburn. [3]
For isotretinoin, avoid concomitant tetracyclines because the label warns of intracranial hypertension with this combination. [6]
For tazarotene, pregnancy is a labeled contraindication; address this independently when reviewing an acne regimen. [5]

sections.heading: Prescribe layered photoprotection rather than sunscreen alone
sections.intro: Select a product with labeled broad-spectrum protection, then pair it with exposure reduction.
paragraphs: Recommend a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher, including on cloudy days. FDA states that broad-spectrum products protect against UVA and UVB radiation and that only broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF at least 15 protects against ultraviolet rays associated with skin-cancer risk and early skin aging. [1][2] SPF is derived from a sunburn test and primarily reflects UVB protection; it should not be interpreted as a complete measure of UVA protection unless the product is labeled broad spectrum. [2]

Counsel that sunscreen is adjunctive, not permission to extend exposure. FDA recommends reducing ultraviolet injury with a combination of sunscreen and other protective measures, and ultraviolet exposure occurs year-round. [1] Protective clothing and avoidance of midday or peak exposure are practical complements to sunscreen use. [8][21]

For patients with a prior sunburn, emphasize prevention of recurrence as a cancer-risk intervention. Unprotected sun exposure increases the risk of skin cancer and early skin aging across all skin colors. [1] Childhood sunburn has been associated with increased cutaneous melanoma risk in a Mendelian-randomization analysis. [15]
bullets: Choose legally marketed sunscreen dosage forms: lotion, cream, stick, gel, oil, butter, paste, ointment, spray, or powder. Wipes, towelettes, body washes, and shampoos cannot be legally marketed as sunscreen dosage forms. [1]
Tell patients not to use recalled sunscreen products; FDA has identified recalls related to benzene contamination while continuing to recommend sunscreen plus other sun-protection measures. [2]
When counseling a patient taking a photosensitizing medication, make sun avoidance and protective clothing central rather than relying only on a higher SPF product. [5][6][8]

subsections.heading: How to explain SPF without overstating it
paragraphs: SPF compares the ultraviolet exposure needed to produce sunburn with versus without the product, so it measures sunburn protection rather than all clinically relevant radiation exposure. [2] Use the broad-spectrum designation to address UVA and UVB coverage, and pair sunscreen with behavioral and clothing-based protection. [1][2]

table.caption: Patient-specific photoprotection counseling.
rows: General outdoor exposure
Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher, even on cloudy days, plus clothing and exposure avoidance. [1][2]
Broad-spectrum SPF 15 or higher addresses ultraviolet rays linked to skin-cancer risk and early aging. [1]
Recent sunburn
Avoid renewed ultraviolet exposure while the skin recovers and establish a preventive routine before the next exposure. [1]
Tanning and sunburn reflect skin responses to potentially damaging ultraviolet radiation. [1]
Topical retinoid or isotretinoin use
Add explicit photosensitivity counseling and reassess a severe photodistributed reaction. [5][6]
These agents carry photosensitivity or increased-sunburn-susceptibility warnings. [5][6]
Infant younger than 6 months
Obtain clinician guidance before sunscreen use. [1]
FDA specifically advises health-professional consultation. [1]

sections.heading: Reassess recurrent or atypical sunburn patterns
sections.intro: Recurrent injury should lead to prevention review and diagnostic reconsideration.
paragraphs: At follow-up after a significant episode, document the exposure setting, medications, photoprotective behavior, and whether erythema or blistering was confined to exposed skin. A mismatch between modest exposure and severe reaction should redirect the evaluation toward photosensitivity or medication-associated phototoxicity. [5][6][16]

For patients receiving phototherapy for atopic dermatitis, recognize that treatment is distinct from incidental sun exposure but has relevant ultraviolet adverse effects. FDA review materials describe phototherapy as an option with a time-intensive in-office schedule and risks that may include actinic damage, sunburn-like reactions, skin cancer, and cataracts depending on modality. [4] New sunburn-like reactions during phototherapy warrant review of the modality, cumulative exposure context, and concurrent photosensitizing treatments.

Use every sunburn encounter to identify preventable future exposure, particularly in patients with repeated burns, retinoid use, or evidence of chronic ultraviolet injury. Regular and proper sunscreen application has been reported to reduce sunburn, photoaging, and later skin-cancer risk, but sunscreen should remain part of a broader exposure-reduction strategy. [14][1]
bullets: Escalate recurrent blistering or severe photodistributed episodes for dermatologic assessment when medication modification and strict ultraviolet avoidance do not explain or control the pattern. [16]
Review sunscreen selection: broad-spectrum status and SPF 15 or higher are the FDA threshold for protection against ultraviolet rays linked to skin-cancer risk and early skin aging. [1][2]
For patients on phototherapy, assess for sunburn-like reactions and ocular-risk counseling because cataracts are listed among potential modality-dependent risks. [4]

table.caption: Follow-up triggers after an acute sunburn episode.
rows: Repeated burns despite reported sunscreen use
Incomplete layered protection or inadequate attention to non-sunscreen measures. [1][8]
Verify broad-spectrum SPF 15-or-higher selection and reinforce clothing and avoidance strategies. [1][2]
Severe reaction after modest exposure
Possible medication-associated photosensitivity or phototoxic eruption. [5][6][16]
Conduct a full medication and topical-product review.
Sunburn-like reaction during phototherapy
Potential phototherapy adverse effect. [4]
Review phototherapy regimen and concurrent photosensitizing exposures.
Progressive blistering or severe cutaneous symptoms on isotretinoin
Potential serious skin reaction requiring urgent evaluation. [6]
Assess immediately and follow product-label safety instructions.
